title: Can a robot camera calibrate itself without a checkerboard, and does it know when it is wrong?
lede: research programme on target-free camera self-calibration on two real cameras: bundle adjustment with the board's geometry withheld lands within 0.15% and 0.24% of Zhang's focal length and shows the board itself bends; over 560 converged view-subset solves the spread of view angles predicts the error (ρ −0.46/−0.58), the solver's σ is about 2× too small (2.4× near the critical set, where Zhang's is 5.8×), and a 0.5% σ gate rejects 92% of bad updates but accepts only 84% of good ones; the 2× is real (rms z 2.28 against the target-free solution), and a leave-one-view-out jackknife σ is honest with no fitted factor (rms z 0.70/0.65) but ranks good and bad updates worse (AUC 0.75 against 0.91); a released-object (bend-aware) Zhang equals target-free BA exactly, and adding k2 leaves σ overconfident (nested rms z 3.01); the 11×11 cornerSubPix window misplaces outer corners by up to 6.4 px, which made most of the apparent 5–9 px flat-board c_y shift (1.2–1.4 px with findChessboardCornersSB), moves Zhang's f by up to 1.3% between OpenCV detectors, and cleaner corners make σ less honest (nested rms z 3.1–3.5); with old and new calibrations from disjoint views, a χ² update test on the solver's covariance fires on 72% of unchanged cameras, and inflated to be quiet (6.5% false alarms) it detects a 1% focal change in 10–12% of splits and a swap to the other camera unit in 30–77%, because each view set carries its own offset (right c_x 4.6× its σ at every size); a leave-one-view-out jackknife covariance makes the test honest with nothing borrowed (1.7–2.5% false alarms) but blind to focal changes under about 4%, and SB corners lift its detection of the real unit swap from 30% to 75%; that blindness is information for the three-parameter test (an oracle threshold still catches a 2% focal change in only 5–10%), but on the focal length alone the χ² reference is about 3× too wide, and a threshold borrowed from the other camera catches a 2% change in 28–41% of splits and 4% in 78–85% at 0–5% false alarms; renders of the real views from a known camera show which corner localiser is right: the printed board’s end squares are half width, which pulls the 11×11 window towards the edge and biases f by +0.4% to +1.5% (real +0.6/+0.9%) and SB’s by −0.3% to −0.4% (real −0.1/−0.4%), while a 5×5 window stays within 0.04% of the truth; rerun on those unbiased 5×5 corners, the f-alone update test catches a 2% focal change in 61% of a 60-split sample (43% once every disjoint split is scored; 34–35% before) and a 1% change in 18–28%, but a threshold borrowed from the other camera then over-alarms on one of them (11%); a threshold from the old calibration’s own 4 + 3 split-halves needs nothing borrowed and stays quiet (0–1% false alarms) but is deaf (0.8% at 2%), because the focal length’s spread does not shrink as 1/n below 5 views; the jackknife's overstatement is a small-set effect (7–8× at 4 views, 1.1–1.4× at 10) while the solver's σ is 2–6× too small at every size, and on every disjoint split a robust (MAD) jackknife against a plain χ² reference catches a 2% focal change from 6 views in 54% of splits at 2.3% false alarms, with nothing borrowed from another camera; but χ²<sub>1</sub> is the wrong reference for that robust test (under independent per-view offsets it would give 6.1% false alarms; the two errors cancel on this rig), and a reference derived from that model, still borrowing nothing, keeps false alarms at 0.2–0.5% and catches the 2% change in 19% of 6-view updates; a reference drawn from a linearisation of the unit's own bundle adjustment (within 0.2% of the nonlinear solver at 4–7 views) lifts that honest figure to 33% at 0.4–1.4% false alarms, and with it the plain jackknife does as well as the robust one; on two more cameras (TUM RGB-D's Kinect and Xtion) that twin reference stays at 0.06–0.80% false alarms with 5–6 new views but over-alarms at 4 (3.3–4.7%), and a 2% change is caught in 10% of 6-view updates, not 33%
summary: A research programme (proposal and log on the project page) on recalibrating a camera from the features it already sees, with no target, and on whether the solver's own uncertainty is honest enough for a robot to accept or reject the update. Milestone 1 uses OpenCV's real stereo calibration photos (two cameras, 13 views each, Apache-2.0): the checkerboard corners are kept as correspondences but the board's geometry is withheld, so the 54 corners become free 3-D points. Started 30% off in focal length, bundle adjustment lands at 534.8 and 538.4 px against Zhang's 535.6 and 539.7 px (gaps 0.15% and 0.24%, under 1σ), with a reported σ 1.12× Zhang's, refuting our prediction of a 2× price for having no target. The free corners leave their best plane by 0.0077 square widths rms (0.024 at most), and the two cameras, solved separately, reconstruct the same bend (correlation 0.90; 0.91 with a second distortion term): the printed board is not flat, which a flat-board model cannot absorb (target-free reprojection error 0.26 against 0.30 px per coordinate). Over 400 random subsets of 3 to 12 views the focal length's z-score against the all-view reference has rms 1.94 (95% 1.75–2.12) for 4–12 views, so the reported σ is about twice too small; Zhang's is no better (2.16). Limits: one rig and board, corners without mismatches, the reference is itself a flat-board fit, and every solve stopped on its evaluation cap. Milestone 2 fixes the solver (gauge pinned, analytic Jacobian, Levenberg–Marquardt: all 560 solves converge, at most 177 evaluations) and confirms milestone 1's rms z (1.945 against 1.944). The largest angle between the views' board normals predicts the focal error (Spearman ρ −0.46 and −0.58), and the reported σ tracks it (ρ +0.39 / +0.45) but stays about 2× too small, 2.4× on 160 near-critical subsets of near-parallel boards. There Zhang's σ is much worse (rms z 5.8) and its focal length is further off (median 1.50% against 1.09% at 4 views). A pre-registered accept gate, σf/f ≤ 0.5%, rejected 92% of updates more than 2% off but accepted only 84% of those within 1%, short of the 90/90 target; an inflation factor fitted on one camera did not transfer cleanly to the other. Milestone 3 asks whether the 2× is real and whether a robust σ fixes it. Scored against the target-free all-view solution with the nested variance, rms z is still 2.28, so the checkerboard reference is not the cause. A leave-one-view-out jackknife (3,480 re-solves) gives an honest σ with no fitted factor: rms z 0.70 and 0.65, 2σ coverage 97–99%, and 1.01 on near-critical subsets where the reported σ gives 2.34; the cluster-robust sandwich helps only on one camera. But the jackknife is very conservative at 4 views (15× the reported σ) and ranks good against bad updates worse (ROC AUC 0.75 against 0.91), so a 0.5% jackknife gate accepts only 19% of good updates: an honest error bar and a good accept statistic are different things. Milestone 5 tests the two suspects milestone 1 named. OpenCV's released-object calibration (a bend-aware Zhang) turns out to be the same estimator as the target-free bundle adjustment: identical intrinsics, σ and board shape to 1e-6 px, because free corners leave the board only its scale. Against it, the flat, evenly spaced board assumption alone moves the principal point cy by 8.7 px (left) and 5.3 px (right) while reporting a 1 px σ. A second radial term k2 is clearly non-zero but does not make σ honest: nested rms z 3.01 (2.00 without five outliers) against 2.28 with k1 alone. Residuals of neighbouring corners stay correlated (0.31 and 0.24), but only along one board axis (0.44–0.56, against about 0 along the other), which points at the board or the detector rather than the lens. Milestone 1's reprojection comparison was corrected here (0.30 against 0.26 px per coordinate, not 0.42 against 0.26). Milestone 6 traces the one-axis residual pattern to the corner localiser used so far: cornerSubPix with an 11×11 half-window (a 23 px box) misplaces corners on the board's outer ring by up to 6.4 px, because the box runs off the pattern. All 26 corners that differ by more than 1 px from a 5×5 window are on that ring. With a 5×5 window or OpenCV's findChessboardCornersSB, reprojection error halves and the one-directional structure mostly goes. This corrects milestone 5: the flat-board shift of cy is 1.2 px (left) and 1.4 px (right) with SB corners, not 8.7 and 5.3; the bend survives, 25–45% shallower and still seen identically by both cameras. The localiser alone moves Zhang's focal length by up to 7.2 px (1.3%), several times any reported σ. And cleaner corners make the reported σ less honest, not more: it halves while the error barely moves, so the nested rms z rises from 2.28 to 3.1–3.5. A sandwich σ clustered by board column does not help (2.44 / 1.72). The four pre-registered hypotheses: one held, three refuted. Milestone 4 turns this into the decision a robot makes. Each camera's 13 views are split into an old set of 7 and a new set of 3–6 other views (60 splits per size and camera, 908 solves), and a χ2 test on (f, cx, cy) decides whether to keep the old calibration, adopt the new one or flag for a target recalibration. On unchanged cameras the test with the solver's covariance fires on 72% of splits (nominal 1%): between disjoint view sets the covariance is 2.3–2.9× too small for f and cy and 4.6× for the right camera's cx, with no fall as views are added. Inflated by the factor measured on the other camera, false alarms drop to 6.5%, but a 1% focal change (an exact model transform of the real corners) is detected in only 10–12% of splits with 5–6 views, and a real swap to the other camera unit (0.67% in f, 17 px in cx) in 30–77%. Even a factor fitted on the scored camera leaves about 4% as the smallest focal change detected most of the time. The rule adopts a harmful update in 1.4% of decisions with the transferred factor and 5.6% without. One of five pre-registered hypotheses held; the splits reuse 13 views, so the intervals are too narrow. Milestone 4b replaces the borrowed factor with a covariance each calibration computes from its own views (8,580 more solves, two corner detectors). A leave-one-view-out jackknife makes the test quiet with nothing taken from another camera: 2.5% false alarms on the old corners and 1.7% on findChessboardCornersSB corners, against 58–74% for the solver's covariance and 36–38% for a sandwich clustered by view. It pays in power: with 6 new views it detects a 2% focal change in 7–12% of splits and 4% in 41–62%. The detector matters as much as the statistics: with SB corners the jackknife test catches the real swap to the other camera unit in 75% of splits, against 30% with the old corners, and harmful adoptions are 0.5–1.5% of decisions. All five pre-registered hypotheses held. Milestone 4c re-tests those stored solves with other thresholds (no new solve). A small-sample Hotelling reference (median 5.9–6.2 degrees of freedom) silences the test completely and keeps only a fifth of its 4% detections; even an oracle threshold fitted on the scored camera detects a 2% focal change in only 5–10% of splits with the three-parameter statistic, so there the limit is information. On the focal length alone the jackknife overstates the variance about 3× (99th percentile of z2 1.7–4.2, not 6.6): against the other camera's 99th percentile it detects a 2% change in 28–41% of splits and 4% in 78–85%, with 0–5% false alarms, close to the oracle, but it cannot see the unit swap, which lives in the principal point. Four of five pre-registered hypotheses held; the f-only power was not pre-registered, and the thresholds rest on 180 statistics from splits that reuse 13 views. Milestone 6b settles which corner localiser is right by rendering each real view again from a known camera at its real pose, with blur and noise calibrated so the renders’ measured edge width (0.95–0.96 px) and noise match the real images’. On a board with full squares all three localisers find the corners to 0.04–0.06 px and the focal length to 0.04%, so four of five pre-registered predictions failed: the real 1% shift is not localiser behaviour on an ideal pattern. The cause, found afterwards: the printed board’s end squares in two of its columns reach only 0.49–0.53 of a corner spacing past the last corner, against 0.94–0.97 elsewhere. Rendered that way, the 11×11 window is pulled up to 9.6 px towards the board’s edge and biases Zhang’s f by +0.4% to +1.5% (real images, against the 5×5 window: +0.64% / +0.91%), findChessboardCornersSB is biased the other way by −0.3% to −0.4% (real: −0.12% / −0.39%), and the 5×5 window stays within 0.04% of the truth. So Zhang on 5×5 corners (532.9 / 536.2 px) is the best focal length for this rig, and earlier milestones carry a localiser bias of +0.6–0.9% (11×11) or −0.1 to −0.4% (SB). Limits: the renders leave out the bend, the clipboard and the sensor’s own noise, and the end-square measurement and ablation were not pre-registered. Milestone 4d reruns the update test on those 5×5 corners (4,290 solves): the focal-length spread between disjoint view sets falls from 0.86–1.02% to 0.59%, and the f-alone jackknife test with the other camera’s threshold detects a 2% focal change in 61% of splits (34–35% on the biased corners) and the real unit swap in 79% (three-parameter test), but the borrowed threshold now gives 11% false alarms on the left camera, because the jackknife overstates the spread 1.5× on one camera and 2.8× on the other. Milestone 4e asks whether a camera can set that threshold from its own old views (3,168 more solves: every 3- and 4-view subset). Splitting each 7-view old set into 4 + 3 in all 35 ways and scaling the halves’ focal-length spread by 1/n gives a test with nothing borrowed that is quiet (0.6% / 0.0% false alarms) but deaf: a 2% focal change is caught in 0.8% of splits. The halves overstate the real old-to-new spread 2.9× and 5.2×, because below 5 views the focal length’s spread falls much faster than 1/n (per view 3.3–5.2% at 3 views, 2.2% at 4, 1.0–1.7% at 5–7, found after the prediction failed). A per-unit threshold needs halves of at least 5 views, about 10 views in the old calibration. Two of five pre-registered predictions held, both only because the test stays silent. Milestone 4f solves every subset of 3 to 12 of the 13 views on the 5×5 corners (16,172 view sets): the jackknife’s overstatement of the focal length’s real spread falls from 7–8× at 4 views to 1.1–1.4× at 10, mostly because a few delete-one solves of a small set land near the critical set, while the solver’s own σ is 2–6× too small at every size. Milestone 4g scores the update test on every disjoint split those solves allow (37,752 per camera, no new solve). The borrowed threshold’s 61% was flattered by a 99th percentile from 180 statistics: on every split it catches a 2% focal change in 43% of 6-view updates (left 56–61%, right 26–30%). A robust jackknife (1.4826 × the MAD of the delete-one focal lengths) is still not an honest error bar (the right camera’s predicted spread is twice the real one), but against a plain χ21 at 1% it catches the 2% change in 54% at 2.3% false alarms, the same rate as the borrowed threshold, evenly on both cameras and with nothing taken from another unit. One of four pre-registered predictions held (the power one); the robust test’s left-camera false alarms, 3.4%, sit just above the 3% bar. Milestone 4h shows that χ21 is the wrong reference for that robust test: if each view adds an independent offset to f, its z2 has a 99th percentile of 18.45 at 7 + 6 views and χ21 would give 6.1% false alarms, so the 2.3% here comes from two errors cancelling. Against a reference derived from that model, which borrows nothing and can be computed for any set sizes, the test stays at 0.45% / 0.20% false alarms but catches a 2% change from 6 views in 18.6% of splits (all three pre-registered predictions held). Milestone 4i takes the reference from the unit itself: linearising its 13-view solve gives every view subset’s first-order response of f to corner error (within 0.2% of 9,600 nonlinear solves at 4–7 views), and drawing the unit’s own residual patterns through it gives each split a threshold (median 10.9 / 12.5 at 7 + 6 views, not 18.45). The twin explains most of the jackknife’s small-set inflation from geometry; against it the robust test fires on 1.44% / 0.37% of unchanged updates and catches a 2% change from 6 views in 33.1% of splits, with nothing borrowed. The right camera’s extra spread, which its twin does not show, keeps it below the pre-registered 0.5% floor (three of four predictions held). With this reference the plain jackknife does as well (34.7%), and one threshold per design nearly as well as one per split (30.8%). Milestone 4j runs the same test, unchanged, on two more cameras from the TUM RGB-D benchmark (a Kinect and an Xtion, 13 views each, 11,442 solves). Self-calibration lands within 0.64% of TUM’s calibration on the Xtion (+1.85% on the Kinect, whose lens needs more than k1). The twin reference stays at 0.06–0.80% false alarms with 5–6 new views but over-alarms with 4 (3.3% and 4.7%), where the delete-one sets are 3-view; a 2% change from 6 views is caught in 10% of splits, because these units fix f less precisely and the cold-start solver falls into far minima on some subsets; and the real 1.4% focal difference between the two units is caught in 6–8%, as often as a scaled change of that size (one of five predictions held).
